newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan says low rate still helping economy.
newsitem.headline: Japan says low rate still helping economy.

text.p: Japan's top financial bureaucrat endorsed the markets' view on Wednesday that the country's low interest rate policy will remain intact for a while, saying it was still having positive effects on the economy.
"We believe the effects of the low rate (policy) are spreading to various sectors (of the economy). It still has positive effects," Vice Finance Minister Takeshi Komura told Reuters in an interview.

He declined to comment on the official discount rate as the decision to change this rested solely upon the Bank of Japan (BOJ), but added that the central bank also held favourable views on how its rate policy was affecting the economy.
The dollar stood above 119 yen in late Tokyo market trading after Komura's comments on interest rates came out, while key Japanese government bond futures prices jumped momentarily.

Pessimism over Japan's economic outlook has spread throughout Tokyo financial markets, as it has become evident that private consumption will take more time to recover from the shock of a national sales tax increase in April.

Asked whether the markets were being too pessimistic over economic prospects, Komura said that long-term interest rates were generally on a declining trend, but that he could not comment on views held by markets.

"The effects of the tax rise were largely within expectations... Private consumption is recovering gradually as well as capital spending. Although the tempo (of the recovery) may slow temporarily, the economy is continuing to recover on the back of firm private-sector demand," Komura said.

The government's monthly economic report released on Tuesday echoed his cautiously optimistic view, saying that the economy was continuing to recover but the pace of the recovery was slowing temporarily from the sales tax increase.

Komura also played down fears among U.S. officials and the markets that the rise in Japan's current account surplus will continue and may have the potential to reignite trade friction with the United States.
The vice minister said the recent rise in Japan's current account surplus was a temporary phenomenon which was unlikely to continue.
Asked if he believed that the surplus would decrease or that the speed of its climb would slow heading into the autumn, Komura said: "I think it (the surplus) will follow that path."

Earlier, in an interview with Reuters Financial Television, Lawrence Greenwood, the economic minister-counsellor at the U.S. embassy in Tokyo, said that autumn was a key period to watch for movements in the trend of Japan's surplus.
